deep.reconstruction:
This page sits in the introduction (§1) and the start of §2 of Grothendieck's preparatory notes for his Nov.–Dec. 1967 IHES lectures on crystals. Those lectures were published as 'Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes' (notes by J. Coates and O. Jussila) in Dix exposés sur la cohomologie des schémas, 1968.

The top two lines finish a sentence from the previous page. That sentence asks to extend the f^!, f_! formalism (as in Hartshorne's Residues and Duality) from complexes with linear differentials to complexes whose differentials are differential operators. In modern terms these are differential complexes in the sense of Herrera–Lieberman and M. Saito. The de Rham complex Ω^•_X is the basic example: its differential d is a first-order differential operator, not O_X-linear.

The paragraph 'Dans b) et c)...' sums up the two desiderata listed earlier, presumably:
- (b) a six-operations / duality formalism for arbitrary separated morphisms of finite type;
- (c) its extension to differential-operator complexes.
Both amount to one question: the definition of the right category of coefficients. That category should contain both coherent (O-linear) complexes, with Hartshorne-style duality, and de Rham-type complexes. The lectures are meant to show the path followed so far towards building such coefficient categories, namely crystals and the crystalline/infinitesimal sites.

In modern language, the answer that history gave in characteristic 0 is D-modules. Complexes with differential-operator differentials are equivalent to complexes of induced right D-modules (Saito 1989). The six operations then come from Bernstein–Kashiwara–Mebkhout, holonomic theory and mixed Hodge modules. In characteristic p (crystalline setting) the answer is Berthelot's arithmetic D^†-modules, with later work by Caro, Abe and Kedlaya.

§2 opens a 'tour d'horizon' on l-adic cohomology for algebraic varieties and its limitations. It asks rhetorically why one should invest so much in a programme of 'algebraisation and generalisation à outrance' of de Rham cohomology when l-adic invariants already exist and serve arithmetic applications such as the Weil conjectures. The next page continues with H^i(X, Z_l) = lim H^i(X_et, Z/l^n) and the comparison isomorphism with H^i(X^an, Z) ⊗ Z_l. The coming argument is the standard motivation for crystalline cohomology: l-adic theories miss p-torsion and p-adic information in characteristic p.
errors: None mathematically; the page is programmatic. It is not a statement of results.

ideas.what: Need for a single 'category of coefficients' containing both coherent O-linear complexes (Hartshorne-style duality) and de Rham-type complexes whose differentials are differential operators, with a full f^!, f_! formalism.
ideas.modern_name: D-modules / differential complexes with six operations; arithmetic D^†-modules in char p
ideas.usually_credited_to: Kashiwara, Mebkhout, Bernstein (D-modules); Herrera–Lieberman, M. Saito (differential complexes ↔ induced D-modules); Berthelot (arithmetic D-modules)
ideas.where_published: Introduction of 'Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes' (Dix exposés, 1968), which discusses coefficients for de Rham cohomology and duality; also Récoltes et Semailles on 'coefficients de De Rham' and the 'crystals' programme

ideas.what: Motivating crystalline/de Rham theory by the limitations of l-adic cohomology in characteristic p
ideas.where_published: Crystals and the de Rham cohomology of schemes, §1–2 (Dix exposés)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a programmatic transition page. The 'category of coefficients' unifying coherent duality and de Rham complexes is a known theme of Grothendieck's: it appears in the published Crystals lectures and in Récoltes et Semailles. It was later realised through D-modules and differential complexes. The explicit pairing of Hartshorne-style f^! with differential-operator complexes as early as 1967 is a nice document, but it is not new to specialists.
